thread.title: The live-work-play HQs that Amazon — and even McDonald’s — embrace could prove pivotal to their growth - MarketWatch

author: Rachel Koning Beals
title: The live-work-play HQs that Amazon — and even McDonald’s — embrace could prove pivotal to their growth - MarketWatch
text:
Amazon’s beauty contest for a highly coveted second headquarters made clear that its future satellite address “could be, but does not have to be” a downtown campus like its Seattle home base. Some of the 20 finalists, locations around Washington, D.C., and Atlanta, for example, would put Amazon’s footprint firmly in the suburbs.
But to rebuff a distinctly urban or urban fringe setting now would be in contrast to the direction that an increasing number of major corporations are taking with doubling down on, and in some cases, moving to, urban zip codes for their headquarters or regional hubs.
Their bet is that talented hires are tired of long commutes and limited or expensive housing, far from city centers. These companies want to sell a lifestyle to current and future employees — millennials, empty-nesters and in-betweeners — with convenient gyms, restaurant options offering mere steps from desk to happy hour and road or rail transportation choices, including parking for staff that gets to work on two or four wheels.
As for Amazon itself, there’s little doubt it helped define the urban tech campus, occupying or building out 8.8 million square feet in Seattle’s mixed-use, high-density South Lake Union neighborhood over the past decade.
What is even clearer is that it’s not just big tech names that think city-smart is the way to attract the next generation of visionary workers that will grow the bottom line.
This spring, McDonald’s MCD, +0.94% officially leaves a sprawling, leafy and car-accessed Oak Brook, Ill., campus that’s been its home for 40 years for Chicago’s once gritty, now trendy Fulton Market. The $250 milllion, 608,000-square-foot development project was led by Chicago-based Sterling Bay, whose separate Lincoln Yards industrial-to-mixed use, 28-acre project along the Chicago River is in the batch of 10 pitches from Chicago and the surrounding area to court Amazon AMZN, +0.99% .
Read: Amazon.com’s ‘HQ2’ finalists include New York, Chicago, L.A., Atlanta, Boston, Dallas, Washington
Opinion: Amazon releases its HQ2 shortlist, and this is what we’ve learned from it
Why downtown, and why now, for McDonald’s, which continues to promote menu revamps and mobile ordering to better align with dining-out trends?
“This world-class environment will continue to drive business momentum by getting us even closer to customers, encouraging innovation and ensuring great talent is excited about where they work,” CEO Steve Easterbrook said as the plans were announced.
Companies including GE Healthcare GE, -1.70% and ConAgra CAG, -1.08% also concluded an that an urban fit was best. Agriculture player Archer Daniels Midland ADM, -1.06% moved its headquarters to Chicago in 2014, after also considering Atlanta, Dallas and Minneapolis. Kraft Heinz KHC, -1.78% left Chicago’s suburbs to run operations out of towering Aon Center near Lake Michigan.
Meanwhile, even farther from Silicon Valley, a major expansion of an urban tech campus was announced earlier this month when Alphabet’s Google GOOGL, +0.92% said it would buy the Chelsea Market building in Manhattan, across the street from its main offices in the old Port Authority building, for as much as $2.5 billion, which would make it the second-most expensive real estate deal in New York history .
And so while the country obsesses over Amazon’s HQ2 search, Google and other tech peers have been quietly transforming many urban neighborhoods into de facto tech campuses , as this City Lab column observed. Twitter TWTR, +1.64% , Uber and Snap also have an established urban presence.
One notable contradiction is of course the shiny new $5 billion Apple AAPL, -0.45% headquarters. Its expanded Silicon Valley footprint deemed “Apple Park” opened earlier this year.
Read: Why Apple’s new campus and Amazon’s HQ2 won’t be neighbors
Don’t miss: People are walking into glass at the new Apple headquarters
A bike path to the front door
Sterling Bay’s managing partner Andy Gloor talked to MarketWatch about the philosophy that drives their high-stakes corporate address changes, which has included a Midwest hub for Google and the Chicago U.S. headquarters for vacuum innovator Dyson.
Urban identities are a bet that the developer backs again this week with its largest purchase yet, a $510 million, 1.65-million-square foot former Montgomery Ward catalog warehouse, co-developed with J.P. Morgan Asset Management JPM, +0.42% that counts Groupon GRPN, +0.23% among its major tenants.
For starters, some companies are rethinking what it means to move downtown, said Gloor. High-rises and a headquarters scattered over multiple floors may no longer cut it. When Hillshire Brands, now owned by Tyson Foods TSN, -0.96% , was sniffing out a Chicago address change, its short list included a couple of floors in Willis Tower, Chicago’s tallest building and a one-time world’s tallest before mostly Asian landmarks took the honors.
Instead, the food company opted for a customized industrial reuse with a communal floor plate (essentially greater open space), their own security measures and a distinct corporate identity in the design, which it saw as a more effective way to do business.
“For some companies and today’s workforce, 100,000 square feet on one floor is better than 10 floors,” said Gloor.
Sterling Bay An interior shot of Tyson Foods-owned Hillshire Brands, where employees grill Jimmy Dean sausages and enjoy a city view from the roof deck. Companies can’t just think 9-to-5, either. Lincoln Yards — which could cost $6 billion to $10 billion to fully build out, the company has estimated — is expected to include a new Metra commuter train station, an extension of the 606 elevated bike trail, a water taxi stop, office and residential towers, a brewery, shops and restaurants. Sterling Bay plans to designate “a substantial amount of acreage” to parks and a wide riverwalk.
The site even includes a proposed stadium for a United Soccer League pro team expansion within three years and can doubly serve as a concert venue.
Sterling Bay Brand it like Beckham In fact, while an extensive effort was taken on by Sterling Bay and city and state officials in the play for Amazon, Gloor is so confident in Chicago’s need to live, work and play in the way that Lincoln Yards provides, he said he’s “agnostic” about securing Amazon. If not the e-commerce giant as its tenant, then on to the next candidate, he said.
Sterling Bay Chicago’s 606 bike path runs right through a proposed urban campus for Amazon at the Lincoln Yards development. Sterling Bay Industrial reuse means there’s room for a proposed Amazon campus of this size in downtown Chicago. Amazon: urban pioneer
As Amazon mulls its options, it remains unclear if the e-commerce giant wants to replicate an urban model.
“The tabula rasa suburban campus is the model that predominates, of course, in Silicon Valley, where hermetic office buildings spread amid parking lots form a landscape of high-end sprawl,” wrote Amanda Kolson Hurley for City Lab . But, she writes, urban planning experts see an opportunity for big-name HQs to also help first- and second-tier suburbs make smart choices about revitalization and expanded public transportation.
Read: 10 U.S. cities with the best growth, employment, and business opportunities
Denver’s largely redacted Amazon bid on view looks to propose sites at a distance from the city center. And Atlanta’s pitch (many analysts give Atlanta a strong chance to win) “includes details for dozens of development sites around metro Atlanta,” according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. The other high-odds contestant from the South, Raleigh itself didn’t exactly make the cut, rather the Research Triangle region did, which encompasses Raleigh, Durham, Chapel Hill, and their suburbs.
As for Amazon, how well the suburbs make themselves appealing to a workforce with attractively priced housing and beefed up transportation options (say with light rail or bus connections or added bike paths) could matter more than an actual address or other incentives. Suburban in-fill over new sprawl could also be an easier pill to swallow for urban planning officials.
Read: Amazon is behind the biggest rent increase last year (and it wasn’t in Seattle)
Sperling BestPlaces has had a fairly good track record with its Amazon handicapping — 15 of its top 20 picks made Amazon’s short list, including its top 11. This time around, it’s putting Atlanta at the top of its list, followed by other areas in the Eastern U.S.
In fact, it’s space, a decidedly non-urban motivation, that Sperling thinks could prompt Amazon in a different direction than what it has in Seattle. “It’s still close enough to D.C., Boston and New York, but Atlanta has more available space to offer, and is affordable,” the analysts said.
The biggest question of where much of the workfoce wants to live and work (and play) may lie with aging millennials.
Joe Cortright, director of City Observatory, has said he expects family-minded millennials to feel the suburban itch not entirely unlike other generations. But, he emphasizes, the voracity with which this savvy group makes that move could look much different.
”At every age, people in this [millennial] generation are more likely to live in cities than were people of earlier generations,” he said. For example, in 1980, 25- to 34-year-olds were about 10% more likely than all adults to live in close-in urban neighborhoods; in 2010 they were about 50% more likely.
Cities must play their part. “The slight decline in the count of aging millennials in some cities is less an indicator of generational disenchantment with urban living than it is an indicator of the failure of our policies to build more housing in the kinds of neighborhoods Americans increasingly value,” Cortright said.
